rows.grounds: instrumental cause of the name Soma

items.question: Why is the prolonged state called Soma and what lies beyond it?
premises: Stirring and bliss lead to a long resting state.
This long resting state is called Soma.
The prolonged state named Pluta is beyond the bliss of Soma.
items.inference: Soma names the long rest born of stirring and bliss, while Pluta is the supreme state beyond even that bliss.
items.plain_english: Because of long rest arising from stirring and bliss, it is called Soma. That supreme state, named Pluta, is established beyond the bliss of Soma.

items.question: What do the knowers of scripture call the light-natured state in the three abodes?
premises: The knowers of scripture call that light-natured state fiery.
This occurs when the three abodes are established.
In that condition only pure light remains.
items.inference: When the three abodes are established, the light-natured state is called fiery and only pure light remains.
items.plain_english: Those skilled in scripture call that light-natured state fiery. Here, when the three abodes are established, what remains is mere light.

items.question: How is the Shiva-bindu described in relation to the letter ma?
premises: Scripture speaks of this as the bindu.
It is regarded as the Shiva-bindu.
It is distinct from the letter ma and bears only its shadow.
items.inference: The Shiva-bindu is taught in scripture as distinct from ma, holding only a trace of it.
items.plain_english: In scripture this is spoken of as the bindu and is regarded as the Shiva-bindu. It is indeed other than the letter ma, bearing only its shadow.

items.question: How do certain consonants transform and what analogy illustrates this change?
premises: The letters ra, la, and ha become established as ṣa, ṇ, ṭha, and visarga.
The letter i can become another vowel by the shadow of a part of ra.
This analogy explains the transformation.
items.inference: Phonemic transformations occur through subtle traces, as shown by the change of i under the shadow of ra.
items.plain_english: Ra, la, and ha become established in the forms of ṣa, ṇ, ṭha, and visarga, just as the vowel i becomes another vowel through the shadow of a part of ra.

items.question: What is the inner desire to emit within the great Lord called?
premises: From the great Lord arises another principle in the same way.
Within him there is an inner desire to emit.
That desire is declared to be the supreme Kauliki power.
items.inference: The Lord's inner impulse to emanate is identified as the supreme Kauliki power.
uncertainties: The sandhi form so@nyo is read as saḥ anyaḥ.
items.plain_english: In the same way, from the great Lord arises another principle. Even while appearing as a vowel in two ways, that inner desire to emit within him is declared to be the supreme Kauliki power.

items.question: What transformation does the supreme Kauliki undergo according to the Trishiras scripture?
premises: The same Kauliki power is stirred.
Through stirring it becomes visarga.
The Trishiras scripture states this in the discussion of kala-pervasion.
items.inference: Stirring transforms the supreme Kauliki into the visarga.
items.plain_english: That very same power, through the force of stirring, certainly becomes visarga. This is said in the Trishiras scripture in the discussion that concludes with the pervasion of kala.

items.question: How is the seventeenth kala described in its nectar-like expansion?
premises: The seventeenth kala has the form of nectar.
It spreads through the movement of the bindu.
That movement expresses its higher and lower nature.
items.inference: The seventeenth kala is a nectar-like power that expands through the bindu's movement between higher and lower levels.
items.plain_english: The seventeenth kala, therefore having the form of nectar, spreads forth through the movement of the bindu of its own higher and lower nature.

items.question: What is the power called when it is devoid of visarga and illuminates all things?
premises: All things are to be illuminated by this power.
When devoid of visarga, that same power is called Shakti-Kundalini.
It is likewise called Prana-Kundalini.
items.inference: The visarga-less illuminating power is identified as both Shakti-Kundalini and Prana-Kundalini.
items.plain_english: When devoid of visarga, that power which illuminates all things is called Shakti-Kundalini, and likewise Prana-Kundalini.

items.question: What names are given to the supreme power at the terminal point of visarga?
premises: At the terminal point of visarga the power is called supreme Kundalini.
It is also called the space of Shiva.
It is called the supreme abode of the self of Brahman.
items.inference: The endpoint of visarga is identified as supreme Kundalini, Shiva's space, and the abode of Brahman.
items.plain_english: But at the terminal point of visarga it is called supreme Kundalini, and also the space of Shiva; it is called the supreme abode of the self of Brahman.

items.question: How is the Lord's visarga described as the play of creation and dissolution?
premises: Mere visarga belongs to the Lord.
It manifests as the play of creation and dissolution.
It is the Lord casting his own self into his own self.
items.inference: Visarga is the Lord's self-reflexive act that appears as creation and dissolution.
items.plain_english: Mere visarga is the Lord's play of creation and dissolution: it is the casting of his own self into his own self, the state belonging to visarga.

items.question: What does visarga become when it is emitted and then contracts?
premises: Visarga is emitted outward.
It then reaches a contracted or dried-up state.
In that state it is defined as Hamsa, breath, consonant, and stop.
items.inference: The emitted and contracted visarga manifests as breath and as consonantal sound forms.
items.plain_english: Visarga, thus emitted and having reached a contracted state, is defined as Hamsa, as breath, as a consonant, and as a stop consonant.

items.question: How are the supreme abode and its visarga identified in this teaching?
premises: The unsurpassed supreme abode is called Akula.
That abode belongs to the Lord.
Its visarga is called the Kauliki power.
items.inference: Akula is the supreme abode, and its emissive aspect is the Kauliki power.
items.plain_english: That unsurpassed supreme abode is called Akula. The visarga of that Lord is called the Kauliki power.

items.question: What happens to the Kauliki power as bliss rises within it?
premises: The state of visarga belongs to that same power.
Bliss rises in a sequence within it.
This unfolding reaches clearly manifest action-power and surges forth.
items.inference: As bliss rises, the power's visarga-state unfolds into manifest action.
items.plain_english: That very same state of visarga, when bliss rises in sequence, becomes a surging forth that extends to clearly manifest action-power.

items.question: How is the expansive nature of visarga illustrated through an analogy?
premises: Visarga draws in and contains a vast range of otherness.
Its form is comparable to something immense and dynamic.
The ocean's endless series of waves provides that comparison.
items.inference: Visarga is like an ocean whose endless waves express its vast contained multiplicity.
items.plain_english: Visarga indeed, having drawn in so much otherness within itself, is like the ocean in this form: an endless succession of waves.

items.question: Why is this visarga called the principle of Kama in the Kula teaching?
premises: This visarga consists of the unmanifest letters ha and ka.
Because of that nature it receives a specific doctrinal name.
In the revered Kula cave it is called the principle of Kama.
items.inference: The unmanifest ha-ka nature of visarga is identified as the Kama principle in Kula doctrine.
uncertainties: The compound śrīmatkulaguhvara is read as a locative doctrinal reference.
items.plain_english: Therefore this visarga, consisting of the unmanifest ha and ka, is called the principle of Kama in the revered Kula cave.

items.question: How is the imperishable unmanifest reality situated in the throat of the beloved?
premises: The imperishable unmanifest is situated in the throat of the beloved.
It has the nature of sound.
It is without desire and free from meditation and concentration.
items.inference: The unmanifest imperishable is a sound-natured presence beyond deliberate yogic effort.
items.plain_english: That imperishable unmanifest, situated in the throat of the beloved, is of the nature of sound, without desire, and free from meditation and concentration.

items.question: What yogic result follows from fixing the mind there, and how is visarga's abiding illustrated?
premises: Fixing the mind there allows one to subdue the world all at once.
Visarga abides clearly in Hamsa.
This clear abiding serves as the model for the teaching.
items.inference: Absorption in that locus grants immediate mastery, just as visarga abides clearly in Hamsa.
items.plain_english: Having fixed the mind there, one should subdue the world all at once. Therefore, just as visarga abides clearly in Hamsa, so too is its state understood.

items.question: How do the phoneme groups abide and emanate from Anuttara?
premises: The principles from Anuttara onward abide from ka to sa.
From Anuttara arises the ka-group.
This emanation is clearly fivefold.
items.inference: The phonemic spectrum from ka to sa abides in Anuttara and emerges first as the fivefold ka-group.
items.plain_english: In the same way, those beginning with Anuttara abide as the range from ka to sa. From Anuttara comes the clear emanation of the fivefold ka-group.

items.question: Why does the fivefold nature appear clearly in each emanation from will-power?
premises: Each emanation is necessarily of the nature of the five powers.
This is clear in every single case.
It arises from will-power abiding in its own single form.
items.inference: The fivefold structure becomes clear in each emanation because will-power expresses its one nature as five powers.
items.plain_english: Because it is necessarily of the nature of the five powers, this is clear in each case, as the power of will, abiding in its own nature, appears from a single form.

items.question: What characterizes the ca-group and what condition leads to the next emanation?
premises: The ca-group is of the nature of the five powers.
It manifests clearly in sequence.
A further emanation is linked to brief activity stained by the knowable.
items.inference: The ca-group unfolds the five powers sequentially, while knowable-stained activity prepares the next phonemic stage.
uncertainties: The long compound in token 6 is compressed and may admit a more technical reading.
items.plain_english: The ca-group is of the nature of the five powers and consists of gradual clear manifestation. Then, through connection with a brief activity that shares in the stain of the knowable, the next stage arises.

items.question: Which phoneme groups arise from the twofold power and from unfolding?
premises: From the twofold power arise the groups beginning with ṭa and ta.
From unfolding arises the pa-group.
Through the pa-group the universe is completed.
items.inference: The ṭa-ta pair comes from duality, and the pa-group completes the manifest universe.
items.plain_english: From that twofold power are born the pair of groups beginning with ṭa and ta. But from unfolding comes the pa-group, because through it the universe is completed.

items.question: Why are the phonemes up to the twenty-fifth called the knowable stop-consonants?
premises: The sequence up to the twenty-fifth has the form of the knowable.
What is knowable becomes clear and manifest.
Therefore this range is declared to have the form of stop consonants.
items.inference: The twenty-five stop consonants represent the clearly manifest knowable domain.
items.plain_english: This, having the form of the knowable and extending up to the twenty-fifth, is clearly manifest. Because it is knowable and thus clear, this much is declared to have the form of the stop consonants.

items.question: How does the power of will give rise to the state of the letter ya?
premises: The power of will exists in two modes, stirred and unstirred.
It turns toward a portion of a different power.
Through that orientation it becomes the state of ya.
items.inference: The letter ya arises when will-power, in its stirred or unstirred mode, inclines toward another power.
items.plain_english: And the power of will, which is twofold as stirred and unstirred, turns toward a portion of a different power and goes to the state of ya.

items.question: How does the same will-power become the letters ra and la?
premises: The same power becomes tinged by the stain of the knowable.
This occurs more quickly as it turns toward what is different.
Through that turning it becomes ra and la.
items.inference: Accelerated orientation toward otherness transforms the same power into the states of ra and la.
items.plain_english: That very same power, more quickly tinged by the stain of the knowable, and turned toward what is different, goes to the state of ra and to the state of la.
